newsitem.title: UK: UK shares seen range trading next week, eye Wall St.
newsitem.headline: UK shares seen range trading next week, eye Wall St.

text.p: The London share market is likely to trade in a narrow range next week as the market keeps its eye on Wall Street amid fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve could push up its short-term interest rates in the near-term.
But continued bid speculation in the financial sector should underpin investor sentiment, preventing any significant downturn, dealers and strategists said.
"I expect to see a re-run of the past week," the head of sales and trading at a large brokerage said.
"There are several stories floating around the market about takeovers in the banking sector which will keep us going but people will be looking over their shoulder to see how the Dow behaves."

"I don't see any selling pressure developing next week unless the Dow tumbles," another senior dealer said. "If anything, the risk is on the upside. If the Wall Street shakes off the jobs data, we could see both markets push higher."

A majority of economists expect the Fed to push up its key short-term funds rate by 25 basis points at its next monetary meeting on July 2 after news on Friday that the U.S. unemployment rate had fallen to its lowest level in 23 years.
Tighter fiscal policy historically has been negative for equities markets but some strategists do not believe a modest rate hike next month will trigger any major sell-off in shares or bonds.
"On balance I think the Fed will probably tighten by 25 basis points in July," said Nick Parsons, economist at Banque Paribas. "Until then, the markets will be choppy."
Parsons said Friday's jobless data would "merely reinforce" prejudices on interest rates and market direction.

"If you believed the Fed was going to tighten then you can look at the figures and prove your case. If you thought the opposite, the same is true. There is something for everyone in the data," he said.
The U.S. unemployment rate in May hit 4.6 percent but average hourly earnings rose by only 0.3 percent on the month versus expectations of a 0.4 percent increase.

"There are still no immediate inflationary pressures out there but the Fed will probably push up rates as an insurance policy. Even so, 25 basis points isn't going to halt a strong U.S. economy," Parsons said.
Interest in financial issues is likely to continue amid speculation that Abbey National Plc and Royal Bank of Scotland could be swallowed up by a bigger rivals in the sector, dealers said.

"Both the Abbey and the Royal Bank of Scotland are seen as firm favourites for a takeover," the head of trading at a large brokerage said. "Also, we should start to see institutions who didn't get their full quota of the Halifax this week start filling their boots."
The Halifax, Britain's largest mortgage lender and one of the ten biggest UK listed companies in terms of market capitalisation, floated on the London exchange on Monday, June 2.

The Halifax's size alone will insure its joins the elite FTSE 100 on June 23. Institutional investors and index tracker funds that failed to gain a sufficient weighting in Halifax shares this past week are expected to start book building ahead of their promotion to blue chip status.

Only a handful of FTSE 100 constituents are due to report results with full-year figures expected from BAA Plc, British Land and Severn Trent Water. The Energy Group is also due to publish its proforma year results -- the first since its demerger from Hanson Plc in February.
Granada Group, meanwhile, is due to publish
six-month figures.

With U.S. jobless data out of the way for another month, British investors will likely concentrate on a batch of UK economic statistics including producer prices, industrial production, unemployment, and retail sales.
In the U.S., retail sales and producer prices are scheduled for release toward the end of the week.
--Dale Faulken, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
